text:
Both sides of the aisle have been negligent in this regard.  Our statement to the committee:  Statement for the Record
Maureen Flatley, President, Stop Child Predators
Submitted to the United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary, Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism
Hearing: "Roblox and Online Gaming: Digital Playgrounds Endangering America's Children"
Date: Tuesday, November 17, 2026
Chairman Hawley, Ranking Member Durbin, and Members of the Subcommittee:
Thank you for the opportunity to submit this statement for the record. Stop Child Predators commends the Subcommittee for asking hard questions of Roblox. The figures behind your August investigation are sobering: Roblox filed 65,381 reports of suspected child sexual exploitation with the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) in 2025, more than double its 2024 total. But those reports are not evidence that the child safety system failed at the platform. They are evidence that the platform did what federal law requires: it identified suspected offenders and turned them over to the authorities.
The failure comes next. Congress has required technology companies to report the bad guys, but it has never given law enforcement the money to investigate those reports. Until that changes, no hearing, lawsuit or new mandate on platforms will put more predators in prison. I also urge the Subcommittee to recognize the role of parents as children's first line of defense.
I. Companies Report. Congress Has Not Funded the Investigations.
Federal law requires online platforms to report suspected child sexual exploitation to NCMEC's CyberTipline, which routes reports to law enforcement. Platforms are filing in enormous numbers: the CyberTipline received more than 36 million reports in 2023. The 61 Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) task forces that receive these tips see the same surge locally. In Wisconsin, CyberTips to the state task force grew from 4,671 in 2021 to 19,767 in 2025.
Funding has not kept pace. Since the PROTECT Our Children Act of 2008, Congress has authorized $60 million a year for the ICAC task forces, yet it has never appropriated that amount. The program received $40.8 million in fiscal 2023 and $39.9 million in fiscal 2024, roughly a third less than Congress itself said was needed, while the reports it must act on multiplied. Congress has since reauthorized the program at higher levels through fiscal 2028, but an authorization is a promise, not a paycheck.
The result is predictable. The Stanford Internet Observatory's 2024 study of the CyberTipline found investigators overwhelmed, with a single detective responsible for as many as 2,000 reports a year. Once a report is referred, nothing requires anyone to investigate it, and no agency publicly tracks how many are investigated or lead to an arrest. A tip that sits unopened in a police queue protects no one. Before the Subcommittee concludes that 65,381 reports reflect a failure by Roblox, it should ask how many of those reports law enforcement had the resources to investigate.
II. Parents Are the First Line of Defense
More than 170 lawsuits against Roblox have been consolidated in federal court in San Francisco, and plaintiffs' firms say thousands more are under investigation. When I hear about a five-year-old groomed through an online game, my first question is not about an algorithm. It is why a five-year-old was alone, unsupervised, chatting with strangers on the internet.
That is not a comfortable question, and I do not raise it to diminish the horror of what these children endured. The predators who target them are criminals and belong in prison. But a culture that responds to every tragedy by searching for a corporate defendant teaches parents a dangerous lesson: that someone else is responsible for watching their children.
The law has never taught that lesson. Every state places a duty of care and supervision on parents and guardians. Child neglect statutes from Alabama to Wyoming recognize parents as the first line of protection for children too young to protect themselves. We do not leave a five-year-old alone at a shopping mall and then sue the mall when a stranger approaches. An online game with more than 100 million daily users is a public place full of adults, too. The same common sense applies.
III. Litigation Is Not Prevention
Mass-tort litigation is a business, and its advertising ("Was your child harmed on Roblox? You may be entitled to compensation") sends a message far beyond any single case. It tells parents the danger was invisible, unknowable and entirely the company's fault. It encourages learned helplessness: the belief that parents cannot reasonably be expected to understand the devices they hand their children, and that the remedy for harm is a check rather than a change in household habits.
Lawsuits cannot do what attention does. Even if every plaintiff in the Roblox litigation prevails, predators will move to the next platform, the next app and the next chat feature, as they always have. A parent who has taught a child to recognize grooming protects that child everywhere. A verdict protects no one in particular.
IV. What Works
The tools to protect young children online are free and widely available. Every major phone, tablet and game console offers parental controls that can disable chat entirely, limit screen time and require approval for new contacts. Beyond the settings, the most effective protections are the oldest ones: devices used in common rooms, not bedrooms; parents who know which games their children play and whom they talk to; and children who have been told, plainly and often, that no one online is allowed to ask for secrets or pictures, and that they will never be in trouble for telling a parent.
None of that requires a law degree or a congressional hearing. It requires attention.
V. Recommendations
Stop Child Predators respectfully urges the Subcommittee to:
Appropriate the full authorized funding for the ICAC task forces. Congress has required companies to report; it must pay for the investigations those reports demand. Fund the task forces at their authorized levels, and scale that funding to the volume of CyberTipline reports they receive.
Require public reporting on CyberTipline outcomes. NCMEC, the ICAC task forces and federal agencies should publish how many reports are referred, investigated and closed, and how many lead to arrests or the identification of a child victim.
Hold platforms to honest safety marketing and prompt cooperation with law enforcement, including complete, actionable reports. These are fair and enforceable demands.
Reject mandatory age verification. It forces families to hand children's faces and government IDs to databases that hackers prize; in 2025, a breach at a Discord vendor exposed the government ID photos of some 70,000 users. It also burdens every American's right to speak and read online without first showing papers.
Use the Subcommittee's platform to speak directly to parents. Tell them plainly that protecting their children online is their job, and that they are capable of doing it.
Conclusion
The greatest safety feature ever invented for children is an engaged adult. No algorithm, no regulation and no jury award can replace one. If we want fewer victims, we should spend less energy teaching parents to look for someone to blame, and more teaching them to look over their children's shoulders.
The platforms are reporting the predators. Congress should fund the people whose job is to catch them.
Thank you for your attention to these concerns. I would welcome the opportunity to assist the Subcommittee in its continuing work.
Respectfully submitted,
Maureen Flatley
President, Stop Child Predators
Sources
U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary, hearing notice: "Roblox and Online Gaming: Digital Playgrounds Endangering America's Children", November 17, 2026.
Subcommittee investigation and 2025 NCMEC report figures: "Senate Opens Formal Investigation Into Roblox Over Child Safety Failures", August 2026.
ICAC authorization ($60 million a year since 2008) and appropriations ($40.8 million in FY2023, $39.9 million in FY2024): "ICAC Funding Gaps and the Federal Child Protection Promise".
Reauthorization through FY2028: RAINN, PROTECT Our Children Reauthorization Act of 2025; Congressional Budget Office cost estimate, S. 539.
Wisconsin CyberTip growth and the 61-task-force network: Wisconsin Department of Justice.
Stanford Internet Observatory, "How to Fix the Online Child Exploitation Reporting System", April 2024; 2023 report total and detective caseload as reported by the Associated Press.
NCMEC referrals to law enforcement are voluntary and carry no investigation requirement: Comparitech, "Child abuse online statistics".
Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation count of 170 pending actions in MDL No. 3166 as of July 1, 2026, as summarized here.
Roblox daily active users (123 million, Q2 2026 shareholder letter), as reported here.

text:
Restoring Digital Resilience — A Conservative Framework to Prevent Cascading Technology Failures in America’s Critical Infrastructure

Wednesday, November 18, 2026
Dr. Joel P. Rutkowski
Policy Paper

Executive Summary

A cluster of major outages in mid-November 2026—affecting the National Security Agency-NSA’s classified internal network (NSANet), Federal Aviation Administration-FAA air-traffic systems, Microsoft 365 (Outlook/Teams), JPMorgan Chase banking platforms, and dozens of major websites via an Optimizely supply-chain attack—exposed deep structural weaknesses. Most were not coordinated cyberattacks but resulted from aging systems overwhelmed by patches, upgrades, software bugs, and third-party dependencies. Some genuine malicious activity occurred (supply-chain malware injection and ongoing AI-enabled threats).  
 
These events reflect decades of increasing system complexity and interconnection. Under conservative principles—national security primacy, limited government, free enterprise with accountability, self-reliance, and fiscal responsibility—the optimal response prioritizes deliberate modernization with redundancy, strengthened supply-chain controls for critical functions, defensive AI capabilities, market incentives, and deterrence rather than expansive new bureaucracy. The best strategy reduces single points of failure and hasty change while preserving innovation.
 
I. Historical Context: From Isolated Failures to Cascading Digital Risk (1960–2026)

Early digital and power systems had limited interconnections. The 1965 Northeast blackout demonstrated cascade potential in the electrical grid from a single relay failure. Y2K remediation in the late 1990s forced widespread software fixes and highlighted dependency risks, largely avoided through focused private-public effort.  
 
From the 2000s onward, internet adoption, cloud concentration, and always-on digital services multiplied incidents. Notable examples include the 2016 Dyn DNS DDoS (disrupting major sites), SolarWinds supply-chain compromise (2020), repeated cloud region failures, and the July 2024 CrowdStrike update that crashed millions of Windows systems and grounded flights. Analyses of major tech failures show a sharp rise in frequency and impact from the 2010s into the 2020s as systems became more concentrated and automated. Small errors (misconfigurations, bad updates, single hardware issues) now propagate nationally or globally because of tight coupling and reduced offline alternatives.
 
 II. Analysis of the November 2026 Events

- NSANet: Temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance and software patching for known vulnerabilities. No evidence of cyberattack; mission-critical functions remained operational due to redundancy; staff arrivals staggered to reduce load.  
- FAA ground stop (~Nov. 13): Triggered by installation of a new router (during copper-to-fiber upgrade) at a remote radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas (with related issues in Texas). Excessive connection attempts flooded the network, destabilizing communications and radar feeds at most en-route centers. Legacy equipment could not absorb the load. FAA later paused similar new router installs.  
- Microsoft 365: ~24-hour global disruption (Outlook heaviest) caused by a software bug introduced in a July networking-related fix, triggered by traffic rerouting and capacity conditions. Microsoft ruled out malicious activity.  
- JPMorgan Chase: Software bug in on-premise hardware systems slowed transaction processing (affecting some counterparties); explicitly not cyber-related.  
-Optimizely supply-chain attack: Unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. Affected snippets for ~178 organizations (including Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Equifax, IKEA, Salesforce). Payload included card skimming, cryptocurrency address swapping, cookie/screenshot theft, and iOS exploit delivery.  
 
Broader context from experts (including former CISA Director Chris Krebs): AI is rapidly discovering vulnerabilities, accelerating patching far beyond historical rates. Patches and upgrades frequently destabilize systems. Adversaries (including state-aligned actors) are also adopting AI for automated attack development. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted new technology layered on old systems overwhelming infrastructure, with high confidence most recent issues were not cyberattacks.
 
III. Root Causes

1. Legacy systems incompatible with rapid modern updates and higher data volumes.  
2. Insufficient testing, validation, and phased/rollback capability for patches and upgrades.  
3. Concentration and single points of failure (one router, one third-party script platform, shared cloud/backend infrastructure).  
4. Weak controls on third-party and supply-chain software embedded in critical or high-traffic systems.  
5. AI-driven acceleration of both vulnerability discovery and exploitation, creating a patching race that introduces instability.  
6. Over-reliance on continuous digital connectivity with limited offline/analog contingencies for essential functions.
 
IV. Guiding Conservative Principles

- National security first: Protect critical infrastructure against foreign adversaries (China, North Korea, Russia, Iran) and criminal actors who exploit digital dependencies.  
- Limited government: Government’s core role is defending the nation and securing truly critical systems; avoid micromanaging private software development or creating large new bureaucracies.  
- Free enterprise and innovation: Private sector drives technological progress. Use incentives, liability, and competition rather than command-and-control mandates.  
- Resilience and self-reliance: Build redundancy, prefer trusted/American-controlled components where security-critical, and maintain contingencies—analogous to energy independence.  
- Personal and corporate responsibility: Operators of critical systems bear primary accountability for reliability.  
- Fiscal responsibility: Targeted, cost-effective measures over open-ended spending.
 
V. Best Strategy to Prevent Recurrence

The most effective approach combines deliberate modernization, targeted security standards for critical functions, defensive AI investment, market incentives, and deterrence:
 
1. Phased modernization with mandatory redundancy and testing for government-owned critical systems (FAA telecommunications, intelligence networks). Require dual-path or failover designs and rigorous pre-deployment testing for upgrades. Extend similar expectations via contracts and liability to private operators of critical private infrastructure (finance, energy, communications).  
 
2.Supply-chain and third-party controls focused on critical uses: Baseline security requirements (code integrity, least-privilege, rapid revocation) for software or scripts embedded in systems that affect national-scale functions. Prefer diversified or higher-assurance vendors; improve transparency without blanket bans on useful tools.  
 
3. AI-aware cybersecurity posture: Accelerate defensive AI tools for vulnerability discovery and validation. Require stronger pre-deployment testing and staged rollout for high-impact patches. Enhance rapid, limited information-sharing between government and private sector (streamlined CISA-style functions).  
 
4. Redundancy and contingency planning: Incentivize or require offline/analog backups and manual procedures for the most essential functions (air traffic, core banking settlement, emergency communications).  
 
5. Deterrence and attribution: Maintain strong capabilities to identify and respond to state-sponsored and criminal cyber operations.  
 
6. Market and fiscal tools: Targeted tax credits or accelerated depreciation for resilience investments (redundancy, secure supply chains, testing infrastructure). Clarify liability so negligence in critical systems has consequences; avoid broad new regulatory agencies.  
 
7. Workforce: Expand practical cyber and systems-engineering training, including through private apprenticeships and focused Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics,-STEM priorities.
 
This strategy stays ahead of the 12–18-month patching surge Krebs and others anticipate while reducing self-inflicted outages.

VI. Pros and Cons of the Recommended Approach

Pros

- Directly addresses observed failure modes (bad upgrades, single points of failure, third-party risk) and reduces cascade potential.  
- Preserves private-sector innovation and speed while imposing accountability mainly where national-scale harm is possible.  
- Strengthens deterrence and long-term American technological self-reliance.  
- Cost-effective relative to repeated major outages or a purely reactive posture.  
- Aligns with existing authorities and public-private models rather than creating new layers of bureaucracy.
 
Cons

- Upfront costs for testing infrastructure, redundancy, and modernization.  
- If testing or staging requirements are poorly designed, they could temporarily slow vulnerability patching and leave windows open to attackers (mitigated by prioritization of critical systems and defensive AI).  
- Some compliance burden on private operators of critical functions; risk of scope creep if not tightly limited.  
- Cannot eliminate all human error, novel AI-enabled attacks, or residual concentration risks.  
- Requires sustained executive and congressional focus amid competing priorities.
 
VII. Implementation Considerations

Immediate after-action reviews of the November incidents by relevant agencies (FAA, NSA, DHS, Treasury for financial sector). Executive guidance and existing authorities can drive near-term changes in government systems and procurement. Targeted legislation could authorize incentives, clarify liability standards for critical operators, and refine information-sharing without expanding bureaucracy. Timeline should track the expected multi-month wave of AI-driven vulnerability patching while sequencing physical modernization (routers, networks, hardware) carefully. Public-private working groups focused on specific sectors can refine technical standards without top-down prescription.

VIII.  Conclusion Discussion and Final Thoughts: Restoring Digital Resilience

The mid-November 2026 cluster of disruptions—NSANet degradation during routine maintenance and patching, the FAA nationwide ground stop triggered by a new router (Juniper, installed by L3Harris during copper-to-fiber work at the El Dorado, Arkansas radio site, with related flooding from an Amarillo, Texas site) that overwhelmed legacy 2001-era Cisco equipment, the Microsoft 365 outage from a latent bug in a July networking fix, the JPMorgan Chase on-premise software bug slowing transactions, and the confirmed Optimizely supply-chain attack injecting malicious JavaScript (card skimming, crypto address swapping, iOS exploits) into snippets for roughly 178 organizations—provides a near-perfect real-time case study validating the paper’s core diagnosis. (https://t.co/efcXid8nhF)

These were not a coordinated cyber campaign. Official statements and early reporting consistently point to internal technical failures, upgrades, capacity issues, and one genuine third-party exploit. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and others emphasized the absence of attack footprints for most incidents, while noting new technology layered onto old systems. The pattern matches the historical trajectory sketched from the 1965 Northeast blackout through Y2K, the 2016 Dyn DDoS, SolarWinds, and the July 2024 CrowdStrike configuration update that crashed millions of Windows systems. Tight coupling, concentration of dependencies, and reduced offline alternatives have turned small errors into national-scale events.

VIII. Root Causes Confirmed and Amplified by AI
The six root causes identified are well-supported. Legacy systems cannot absorb modern traffic volumes or rapid change (FAA’s copper-to-fiber and ancient routers being the clearest example). Insufficient testing, validation, staged rollout, and rollback capability turned routine upgrades into outages. Single points of failure and concentration (one router class, one experimentation platform serving major brands, shared backends) amplified impact. Weak supply-chain controls enabled the Optimizely injection. Over-reliance on continuous connectivity left few graceful degradation paths.

AI acceleration is the force multiplier. Former CISA Director Chris Krebs has publicly described AI agents discovering vulnerabilities at a pace that risks overwhelming patching teams, with windows as short as six to nine months before adversaries possess similar tools. Broader 2026 reporting documents autonomous multi-agent frameworks performing differential analysis of patches, generating and testing exploits with minimal human involvement. Discovery velocity has collapsed timelines that once measured in months to hours or days, while median enterprise patching remains measured in weeks. This creates a structural race in which the act of patching itself becomes a reliability hazard—exactly as observed in the Microsoft latent defect and FAA router behavior. The paper correctly frames this as both a vulnerability-discovery problem and an instability problem.

IX. Evaluating the Conservative Framework

The recommended strategy is coherent and proportionate. It prioritizes national-security primacy for truly critical systems (FAA telecommunications, intelligence networks, core financial settlement, energy and communications) while rejecting expansive new bureaucracy. Phased modernization with mandatory dual-path/failover designs, rigorous pre-deployment testing, and staged rollouts directly targets the observed failure modes. Extending expectations via contracts and clarified liability to private critical operators leverages free enterprise and accountability rather than command-and-control. Focused supply-chain baselines (code integrity, least privilege, rapid revocation) for high-impact third-party components address Optimizely-style risks without blanket bans on useful tools. Defensive AI investment, enhanced but limited information-sharing, offline/analog contingencies for essential functions, and targeted fiscal incentives (tax credits, accelerated depreciation) for redundancy and testing infrastructure are practical and fiscally disciplined. Deterrence and workforce measures complete the picture.

Strengths are clear. The approach reduces cascade potential and single points of failure while preserving innovation speed for non-critical systems. It aligns with existing authorities and public-private models. It is cost-effective relative to repeated multi-billion-dollar outages (CrowdStrike’s estimated Fortune 500 impact alone was on the order of $5.4 billion). It treats resilience analogously to energy independence: deliberate diversification, redundancy, and self-reliance rather than permanent dependence on fragile, concentrated digital paths.

Limitations and trade-offs are also real and honestly noted in the paper. Upfront costs for testing infrastructure and modernization are non-trivial. Poorly designed staging requirements could slow critical patching and enlarge the AI-driven exposure window—an especially acute risk given the current discovery-to-exploit compression. Scope creep remains a perennial danger if “critical” is defined loosely. Residual risks of human error, novel AI-enabled attacks, and concentration cannot be eliminated. Sustained executive and congressional attention will be required amid competing priorities. These cons do not invalidate the strategy; they define the conditions for its successful execution: tight prioritization of the highest-impact systems, defensive AI to accelerate safe validation, and disciplined boundaries on government role.

X.  Broader Implications and Path Forward

The November events illustrate a deeper civilizational challenge. Digital systems have become the nervous system of critical infrastructure, yet they were largely built for availability and features rather than graceful degradation under stress or adversarial pressure. The same dynamics that produce rapid innovation also produce fragility when change is continuous and tightly coupled. Adversaries (state-aligned actors and criminals) will continue to exploit both genuine vulnerabilities and the instability created by rushed remediation. Public trust erodes when banking, air travel, email, and classified networks fail in close succession for mundane technical reasons.

Implementation should begin immediately with after-action reviews of the specific incidents (FAA router behavior and network absorption capacity, Microsoft latent defect, Optimizely access path, NSANet maintenance sequencing). Executive guidance and procurement rules can drive near-term changes in government systems. Targeted legislation can clarify liability for negligence in critical functions, authorize incentives, and refine information-sharing without creating new agencies. Public-private sector working groups should refine technical standards for redundancy and testing rather than prescribe architectures top-down. Sequencing is essential: prioritize the AI patching surge over the next 12–18 months with defensive tools and staged rollouts, while carefully modernizing physical and network layers (routers, fiber, hardware) to avoid repeating the El Dorado-style cascade.

Market incentives and accountability will outperform pure mandates. Operators who invest in dual-path designs, rigorous testing, and higher-assurance supply chains should face lower liability and enjoy competitive advantages; those who do not should bear the consequences of national-scale harm. Analog and offline contingencies for the most essential functions (air traffic communications, core settlement, emergency coordination) should be treated as deliberate insurance, not nostalgia.

XI.  Final Thoughts

The paper’s central insight holds: the optimal response is deliberate modernization with redundancy, strengthened controls where national-scale functions are at stake, defensive AI, market mechanisms, and deterrence—not a new bureaucratic superstructure or a return to isolated systems. The November 2026 cluster was largely self-inflicted. That is both sobering and actionable. It means many future incidents are preventable through better engineering discipline, architectural choices that limit blast radius, and realistic recognition that patching itself has become a high-risk activity in an AI-accelerated environment.

No strategy eliminates residual risk. Human error, novel attacks, and residual concentration will continue. What is avoidable is the current pattern in which routine change repeatedly produces national disruption because systems lack sufficient testing, failover, and contingency. Aligning incentives, focusing government effort on truly critical functions, and treating resilience as a core design requirement rather than an afterthought offers the highest-leverage path. The alternative—continued accumulation of tightly coupled, poorly tested, third-party-dependent systems—guarantees more frequent and more severe cascades as AI further compresses both attack and remediation timelines.

The events of mid-November 2026 are a warning, not an inevitability. Execution of the recommended framework, disciplined by the stated conservative principles of limited government, accountability, and fiscal responsibility, can restore meaningful digital resilience while preserving the innovation that remains America’s decisive advantage.

text:
Every source, what it carries, and how far it can be pushed.

Daniel Ayana, “The ‘Galla’ that Never Was: Its Origin and Reformulation in a Hinterland of Comparative Disadvantage,” *Journal of Oromo Studies* 17(1), 2010, pp. 1–40. The central modern study: the Somali *gaal* etymology, the 1332 and 13th-century attestations, the eliminations, the argument about Bahrey. Peer-reviewed, Oromo Studies Association. Its lexicographic and documentary evidence is strong; its 9th–13th-century chronology, its dating of the Qanana story, its reading of Bahrey's motive and its charge against Lewis's motives are inference, and are flagged as such above.

Brian J. Yates, “Invisible Matter: ‘Galla’ in Ethiopian and European Imaginations,” same issue, pp. 41–86. “There is no interpretation of the term ‘Galla’ in the Oromo language” (p. 42); the Häbäsha attribution (p. 42) — which contradicts Ayana in the same volume; Bahrey (pp. 47–49); the chroniclers and the Europeans (pp. 52–55, 69–70).

Tsega Etefa, “A Great African Nation: The Oromo in Some European Accounts,” same issue, pp. 87–110. The European writers who used the self-name; d'Abbadie's and de Salviac's titles (p. 88, n. p. 105).

G. W. B. Huntingford, *The Galla of Ethiopia: The Kingdoms of Kafa and Janjero* (International African Institute, *Ethnographic Survey of Africa*, 1955), Nomenclature, p. 11. “The origin of the name Galla is uncertain”; the self-name; the d'Abbadie report; the Sidama and “wandering” suggestions; the dismissal of the Prophet story; the dating to Bahrey. The Greek *gala* guess sits in his section on physical characters.

Richard Burton, *First Footsteps in East Africa* (1856) — read in full. Ch. IV. The primary source for the Prophet story — which he calls a “philological fable” — the chief Ullabu and “Kal la pronounced Gal la”; Johnston's “Calla”/blackness derivation and Burton's rebuttal; and the river Gala in Guragé, of which he writes “there is little to find fault with in their theory.” Also the descent stories — the princess “given in marriage to a slave,” and “Metcha, Karaiyo, and Tulema, three sons of an Æthiopian Emperor by a female slave” — and, in the later chapters, the Somaliland material: “These are all remains of Galla settlements”; “the work of an earlier race, probably the Gallas”; “The Somal assert that ten generations ago their ancestors drove out the Gallas from Berberah”; “The Gallas revere it and plant it over sacerdotal graves”; and the Oromo name for Harar, “by the Gallas ‘Adaray’.”

James Bruce, *Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile* (1790), vol. I, bk. II, ch. 2. The earliest claim that the word is Oromo: “These are the Galla, the most considerable of these nations”; “This word, in their own language, signifies Shepherd.” Read with its context — the same passage wonders whether they are “a part of that great Gaulish nation so widely extended in Europe and Asia,” and its footnote 21 has them calling themselves “Agaazi, or Agagi,” the Ge'ez term rather than an Oromo one, citing Purchas.

Morgan J. Smeads, “Abyssinia — The Galla Language,” *Bibliotheca Sacra* 6:24 (Nov 1849), pp. 747–748. An early independent witness to two of the explanations: “The name Galla, according to Bruce, signifies *shepherds*” — which checks out against Bruce's own text, above — and “Mr. Tutschek derives it from the verb *gala*, in their language, which signifies *to go home*, or *to seek a home*” — the Tutschek etymology in circulation five years after his dictionary. The remainder of the article is paywalled and has not been read.

J. L. Krapf, *Vocabulary of the Galla Language* (London: printed for the Church Missionary Society, 1842; Krapf's own bibliography dates it 1840). The earliest lexicon in this file, read in full. The entry *Galla, n. gent., ormo ; orma.* “This is a —,” *kuni ormoda*; the absence of any verb *gala*; and the only *galla* in the book, “Provisions, s. *galla*.” Preface signed C. W. Isenberg. With his *Outline of the Elements of the Galla Language* (1840) and the Galla Gospels of John and Matthew (1841), this is where printing in Oromo begins.

J. L. Krapf, *Travels, Researches, and Missionary Labours During an Eighteen Years' Residence in Eastern Africa* (Boston: Ticknor and Fields, 1860) — read in full. Ch. VI, “Ormania and the Gallas,” p. 61: “They call themselves ‘Orma,’ or ‘Oroma,’ strong, or brave men”; *Afan Orma*, “the mouth of the Ormas”; “The name ‘Gallas’ in their own language means immigrants, and has been given them by the Arabs and Abessinians”; and the coinage — “I propose to include both under the designation of Ormania,” with “To my mind Ormania is the Germany of Africa.” Also the Kenyan-coast origin account, that “the Galla, Wakamba, and Wakuafi had one common father, whose eldest son was called Galla,” and the bibliography of his own works in the appendix on the literature of Abyssinia.

I. M. Lewis, “The Galla in Northern Somaliland,” *Rassegna di Studi Etiopici* 15 (1959), pp. 21–38. The dissent: “no secure evidence has yet been adduced in proof of this theory” (p. 23); *gal*/*galo* as “pagan, infidel, or non-Muslim in general,” distinct from *Gallawi* (p. 23); Andrzejewski's gloss of Amharic *galla* as “subjects those under government” (p. 22, n. 5); Cerulli (1931, p. 154) read as deriving Somali *gal* from the name, the reverse of Ayana's reading (p. 23, n. 1); “tentative in the extreme” and the warning against projecting names backwards (p. 38).

Lewis's article is also the source for the Somaliland evidence: the stone mounds “loosely referred to as ‘Galla graves’” and the radiocarbon result — “not more than two hundred and fifty years old and probably contain[s] Somali remains” (p. 23); the Somali terms *Gallawi* and *Qot* (p. 22); the displacement sequence (pp. 30, 36–37); and his statement that “Galla” is first recorded only in the late sixteenth century (p. 38), which contradicts Ayana's 1332 reading.

Mohammed Hassen, *The Oromo of Ethiopia: A History 1570–1860* (Cambridge, 1990) — read in full. Its preface, p. xi, carries the four sentences this thread tests: “This was a name, applied by outsiders, by which the Oromo were known until recently”; “The term is loaded with negative connotations”; “The Oromo do not call themselves Galla and they resist being so called”; “In this study I employ Oromo, the name which they have always used.”

Audited, because it is load-bearing. None of those four sentences carries a footnote. Three are defensible — “applied by outsiders” is precisely Krapf's position in 1860. The fourth, *“the name which they have always used,”* is a universal historical claim the book never evidences: across its whole apparatus it names no pre-nineteenth-century source using “Oromo,” and every early source it quotes says Galla. Two pages on, at p. xiii, it concedes: “We do not know when the Oromo evolved their separate national identity and language.” The two sit badly together.

And in fairness, which an audit also owes him: the gap works against his own case, not for it. His bibliography does list Tutschek's *A Galla Dictionary*, Munich 1844 — the very book whose headword *oromo* reads “the name by which the Gallas call themselves,” which would have proved what the preface merely asserts. He had it on his shelf and did not cite it at the point of claim. (Krapf's *Travels* of 1860 is listed too; Krapf's *Vocabulary* of 1842, which also carries the evidence, is not.) Someone writing propaganda uses what is in his own bibliography. Elsewhere he is a hard critic of his own side: he challenges Tasaw Merga, an Oromo scholar, on slave figures; rejects an Oromo tradition about a founder, noting the tradition “makes it very clear that Adam in fact was not a historical figure”; flags “an element of self-aggrandisement” in a quoted Oromo official; and says Massaja “may have overstated Abba Bagibo's determination to unite the Oromo.” The verdict is under-evidenced in one sentence, not dishonest — and the sentence is one he could have supported.

Jeylan Wolyie Hussein, “A Critical Review of the Political and Stereotypical Portrayals of the Oromo in the Ethiopian Historiography,” *Nordic Journal of African Studies* 15(3), 2006, pp. 256–276. The pejorative status and the four epithets (pp. 261–262), citing Sorenson (1993: 60) and Debella & Kassam (1996); and the qualification at pp. 268–269 on Oromo elites within the system.

Antoine d'Abbadie, “Sur les Oromo, grande nation africaine désignée souvent sous le nom de ‘Galla’ : lecture faite à l'assemblée générale du 5 avril 1880.” The source of the war-cry report, and of the title that undercuts it.

*The Galla Spelling-Book* (Swedish Mission Press, Moncullo near Massowah, 1894), both title pages, read in the scanned original in the EFS historiska arkivet under “Books in Oromo.” The English page: “by Onesimus Nesib, A NATIVE GALLA.” The facing Oromo page: *afaan Oromoo* and *warra biyya Oromoo*. The single document that settles the self-name question in both directions — and that shows Bulcha's rendering of the title as “the Oromo Reader” to be his own.

*Missions-Tidning* (the whole volume) — all 90 pages of the Sept–Dec 1893 volume OCR'd and searched: 620,584 characters, 127 occurrences of *galla* and its compounds, zero of *Oromo* or *Orma*. It carries a second, unquoted Onesimos letter (Moncullo, 23 May 1893) and Hylander's report that “Onesimus har nu gifvit gallamissionen en ordbok.” The OCR of Fraktur Swedish is imperfect and the counts are approximate, but the control is sound: the same pass finds *galla* 127 times.

*Missions-Tidning*, Evangeliska Fosterlands-Stiftelsen, Stockholm, 1893, pp. 149–150 — Onesimos's letter from Geleb, 28 July 1893, read here in the original Swedish from the scanned volume in the EFS historiska arkivet. The source of the *gallaspråk* sentence and of the six other uses, and the proof that the “(Oromo)” in the modern quotation is editorial.

Charles Tutschek, *Dictionary of the Galla Language*, published by Lawrence Tutschek (Munich, 1844) — read in full. The most direct witness: the preface on the name coming “from their own language, and not from the Abyssinians,” the derivation from the verb *gala*, “to go home,” and “their calling themselves by this same name”; the lexicon's own entries for *gala* as verb and noun; and the four named Oromo informants. Caveats in the post: the preface is the editor brother's, its historical dating is wrong, and *galla* is not a headword for the people.

Charles Tutschek, *A Grammar of the Galla Language*, ed. Lawrence Tutschek (Munich, 1845) — read in full, and the source of the strongest evidence in this thread. Its closing reading texts are letters in Oromo between Tutschek's Oromo students, printed with facing English. P. 90, headed “5. Answer to the foregoing,” signed *Akafed'e Agaf* and dated Munich Oct. 21st 1840: *Gallan gudumtu…*, “Many Gallas who went from the hands of their mothers and fathers sit with weeping hearts.” P. 91, signed *Akafed'e Dalle*: *Wacayon kad'ad'u, ini Galla ziti ha ergu*, “Pray to God, that he may send thee a Galla.” Both pages were located by full-text search and then read off the page images, not taken from OCR. The Grammar also carries *orma* glossed “foreign” and the vocative *ya Gallan!*, and offers no etymology of the name anywhere.

Enrico Cerulli, *The Folk-Literature of the Galla of Southern Abyssinia*, Harvard African Studies III, 1922. The primary evidence on self-use: the notes to Song 15 — “the word galla meaning ‘errant,’ ‘wandering,’ is especially noteworthy”; “probably connected with the Somali root gal meaning ‘stranger’ and afterwards, ‘non-Moslem’”; and the credit to Reinisch as the first to propose the link. Cerulli never states which way the borrowing ran, which is the root of the whole Ayana–Lewis disagreement.

Mekuria Bulcha, “Onesimos Nasib's Pioneering Contributions to Oromo Writing,” *Nordic Journal of African Studies* 4(1), 1995, pp. 36–59. Onesimos as “nama biyya Oromoo” (p. 37); *Macafa Qulqulluu* (1899) and *Jalqaba Barsiisaa* (1894, with Aster Ganno) (p. 40); “the Oromo do not call themselves by that name” (p. 36 n. 1).

Leo Reinisch, *Die Somali-Sprache II: Wörterbuch* (Wien: Alfred Hölder, 1902), p. 167 — the volume Cerulli's footnote 30 points to, located and read in the full-view Harvard scan (hvd.32044099876625) through HathiTrust's own text-only rendering. ❝ Gāl … *jeder nicht-muslim, heide, jude oder christ* ❞, with the Arabic source glossed in Latin as *exules* and *ii qui Muhammedanis tributum solvunt*, and the example *hábaši ó dami wā gálo*, “all Abyssinians are non-Muslims.” ❝ Gāla … (*id., s. gāl*) *die nation der Galla* ❞. The direct page image is blocked to automated access; the transcription above is HathiTrust's text layer, not a reading of the page by eye, and is flagged as such.

Hiob Ludolf, *A New History of Ethiopia* (London, 1682; the English of the *Historia Aethiopica* of 1681) — read in full. Searched end to end for the name: no etymology anywhere. What it does have is Ludolf's attribution — “They are called Galla, briefly by the Habessines: we give them the name of Gallan” — his reason for changing the spelling, “lest while we discourse the Barbarism of the Galli, we should injure one of the Politest and Civilest Nation in the World,” a slave-revolt origin story (“A certain number of Servants being cruelly handled by one Matthew a Nobleman, Revolted”), and, in bk. I ch. XV, fourteen words of the Oromo language from Abba Gorgoryos — none of them a name for the people.

Also carried: Bahrey, *Zenāhu la-Galla* (1593); Cerulli, *Folk-Literature of the Galla*, p. 26; Beke, *On the Origin of the Gallas* (1848), p. 3; Markham (1869), p. 40; Cecchi, vols. II–III; Soleillet (1886); Luling (1987); Asma Giyorgis, *History of the Galla and the Kingdom of Sawa* (Bairu Tafla, trans., 1987); Manoel de Almeida and James Bruce, as quoted by Yates; Hultin (1996), “Perceiving Oromo: ‘Galla’ in the great narratives of Ethiopia,” in Hussein's references and directly on this question.

The test, now run, and what it can and cannot support. All 88 pages of *The Galla Spelling-Book* (1894) were rendered at 300 dpi and put through Ge'ez optical character recognition; every page returning a candidate was read by eye at 400 dpi. Confirmed: ኦሮሞ on the Oromo title page, and twice more in running prose on printed page 77 — *kan Oromootaa* and *Oromoonni*. ጋላ twice in the volume, neither of them the name of a people: the syllabary drill on page 7, and a common noun on page 140 (Krapf's 1842 vocabulary gives *gala* for camel). The recognition is poor on 1894 type and does not spell either word reliably — on the title page it wedges a spurious character into the middle of ኦሮሞ — so the software was used only to point at pages, and every reading here came off the page by eye. These are confirmed occurrences, not a complete census. Anyone with better Ge'ez recognition should redo it.

Not consulted directly, and nothing here rests on them: Mohammed Hassen, *The Oromo and the Christian Kingdom of Ethiopia: 1300–1700* (2015), pp. 66–68, 85, 104–106 — paywalled, cited from its catalogue references; Cerulli (1931), p. 154, which Lewis cites and which has not been read here — though Cerulli's 1922 wording, which has, suggests the ambiguity is his own; and Cerulli (1931) — now identified in full from Ayana's note 20 as “Tradizione storiche e monumenti della Migiurtinia,” *Africa Italiana* 4 (1931), p. 154 — the page Lewis cites for the claim that Cerulli derived Somali *gal* from the name, the reverse of Ayana's reading. That article has not been read here, and it is the single most useful thing left for anyone with library access to check. Reinisch's *Wörterbuch* is no longer on this list: it has been found and read, above.

text:
🚨 THEY WERE DRILLING INTO A BURNING LANDFILL AND IT BLEW A GEYSER OF METHANE AND ROTTING GARBAGE INTO THE SKY!

Chiquita Canyon, Monday a little after 4 PM. Crews were putting in a new well, about 150 feet down into the trash according to County Fire, and they hit a pressurized pocket.
Gas and garbage came blasting straight out the top.
And that well was supposed to be part of fixing the heat problem down there.

So the fix is what blew up.

Hazmat had to decontaminate six workers and four of them got taken to the hospital as a precaution.
Val Verde and a couple other Castaic neighborhoods got told to be ready to leave, and people out there are talking about burning eyes and throats.

They didn't get it capped till around 11 that night.

This dump's been cooking underground since 2022. The EPA called it an imminent and substantial endangerment to the neighborhoods around it, the state put its own order on it in April 2025, it stopped taking trash New Year's Day 2025, and Bonta sued the owner last month.
The owner's Waste Connections, out of The Woodlands, Texas.

Four years of this and they're still the ones holding the drill.

Then County Public Health had to order the company to put neighbors up in hotels. Residents told KTLA nobody from the landfill had even reached out to them.

If you live out there and you're smelling it, call Chiquita and ask for the relocation help, the county ordered them to offer it. Report every odor to South Coast AQMD at 1-800-CUT-SMOG because that's how violations actually get written. Keep the windows shut, and if your eyes or throat are burning don't sit there and tough it out, get somewhere with clean air and get checked. And get on the county's Genasys alerts so you're not hearing about the next one from a news chopper.

Who's signing off on these drilling plans before they punch the next hole?

Full breakdown on my page 👇

NVIDIA just had a record quarter and its board said no to bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO. 🟢

Here's the full picture:

📊 The earnings (Q3 FY27):
🔹 Revenue: $115.8B (+103% YoY)
🔹 Data center: $107.6B (+110% YoY)
🔹 Net income: $65.3B (GAAP)
🔹 Q4 guidance: ~$130B, assuming no China data center compute revenue

🏛 The leadership story:
🔹 Nov 12: Huang resigned as CEO and board member
🔹 Huang then publicly offered to return if the board believed it would benefit shareholders and employees
🔹 Nov 17: Board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call: "The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
🔹 The board accepted the resignation unanimously
🔹 CFO Colette Kress stays interim CEO, and Heidrick & Struggles is leading the search for a permanent one
🔹 A new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee has been created

NVIDIA's release gave no reason for the resignation, and the board declined to discuss the circumstances or its ongoing independent investigation.

My takeaway: record numbers don't remove key-person risk. When a company's identity is tied to one leader, even a $115B quarter doesn't settle the succession question.

text:
The Trump administration’s response to a wave of disruptions affecting banking, air travel, email and even the NSA’s classified network is turning into a dark comedy.

🔹 Marco Rubio, asked whether AI played a role: “I don’t want to speculate.”

🔹 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin questions how there can be so many coincidences, then offers a theory from “one guy that’s very smart with tech.” AI, apparently, is finding so many vulnerabilities that the rush to patch them is overwhelming old systems. Mullin says he’s 98% certain there’s no cyberattack. Apparently, the other 2% is being handled by an anonymous guy.

🔹 Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton points to government agencies and companies upgrading their systems at the same time.

🔹 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy calls it a “head-scratcher,” then reveals that the FAA is still relying on 25-year-old routers and infrastructure dating back to the 1980s. Nothing like discovering your air traffic system is running on technology old enough to collect Social Security.

🔹 And Donald Trump? “It’s life. Things like that happen. It’s fine.”

So there you have it: don’t speculate, trust the anonymous tech guy, blame simultaneous upgrades, scratch your head—and relax. The president says it’s fine.

Americans need facts, a coherent explanation and clear guidance about what to do. Instead, they’re getting a collection of disconnected sound bites from an administration that seems unable to communicate with one voice when it matters most.

The outages may have different causes. The communications failure has one source: the White House.

text:
Ramon Sosa's wife offered $2,000 to have him killed, using his own jewelry as payment and counting on his life insurance. The hitman warned Ramon instead. Police staged his death, tied his hands and photographed him in a shallow grave with a fake bullet wound. His wife laughed at the photos, celebrated and paid the rest. She got 20 years in prison. Ramon forgave her.

In the video below Ramon Sosa tells the full story of how he faked his death to catch his wife.

He met Lulu in 2007. She was a mother of two from Mexico City. Beautiful. Great dancer. At the wedding her mother whispered in his ear: "Now she's your trouble."

They built a boxing gym together. Business was going well. Once she had legal status and saw the money, Ramon felt she didn't need him anymore.

A young man named Mundo overheard Lulu and her daughter in the gym office talking about someone in Mexico who chops people up for money. The next day he called Ramon. Ramon thought he was joking. Mundo said he'd seen the look in people's eyes when they want someone dead.

Police sent in an undercover officer as a fake hitman. Lulu confirmed on tape she wanted Ramon dead. Said she didn't care how. Handed over his watches and wedding bands as a down payment for his own murder.

Ramon was driven to a dump site in a blacked-out SUV. They put death makeup on him, threw dirt on his body and photographed him in a dug grave. He said he walked on his own gravesite.

When the officer showed Lulu the photos she asked: "He won't wake up anymore?" Then started celebrating like she'd hit the lottery.

Police went to the gym posing as missing persons investigators. She denied everything. That was the last piece. She was arrested on the spot.

At sentencing Ramon forgave her in a packed courthouse. She never looked at him once.

Was Ramon saved by luck, or by the one person in the room who decided to pick up the phone?

text:
Parliament, LSU partner to establish MPs’ Academy

Parliament has partnered with Lupane State University (LSU) to establish the Zimbabwe Parliament Academy (ZIPA), a training institution aimed at strengthening the knowledge, skills and capacity of Members of Parliament (MPs).

The partnership was formalised through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding at the New Parliament Building in Mt Hampden. Speaker of Parliament Advocate Jacob Mudenda signed on behalf of Parliament, while LSU was represented by Vice-Chancellor Professor Pardon Kuipa.

Adv Mudenda said the academy seeks to equip MPs with the competencies required to effectively carry out their legislative, oversight and representative responsibilities. He noted that Parliament comprises members from diverse educational, professional and social backgrounds, making continuous training and skills development essential.

Through the partnership, LSU will help ZIPA offer accredited certificate, diploma and undergraduate programmes, subject to regulatory approval. The university will also assist in reviewing existing training modules, developing new programmes and strengthening teaching, assessment and quality assurance systems.

Prof Kuipa said the partnership reflects the evolving role of universities in supporting national development and key public institutions. He said the collaboration would combine Parliament’s legislative mandate with LSU’s academic expertise to enhance governance and democratic processes.

The establishment of ZIPA is expected to contribute to higher professional standards and improved effectiveness within Zimbabwe’s legislature.

text:
US Cancer Patient’s Hijab Question Draws Global Support From Muslim Women
Washington: Jacey Abbott, a 42-year-old mother of three from Bay Minette, Alabama, who is battling stage 4 metastatic breast cancer, asked Muslims on the social media platform Threads whether she could wear a hijab despite not being Muslim. Her question received an overwhelming response from Muslim women around the world, who offered reassurance, styling advice, free scarves and prayers.
Abbott was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2019 and lost her hair during treatment. She found wigs uncomfortable because they caused heat, sweating and itching, while the hijab she bought felt soft and comfortable. However, she worried that wearing it as a non-Muslim might be disrespectful to Muslim women who wear it for religious reasons.
“Can I wear a hijab or is that disrespectful? I have terminal cancer and wigs get so hot and itchy,” Abbott wrote in her post. The message quickly went viral, receiving nearly 100,000 likes and thousands of replies, most of which encouraged her to wear the headscarf.
Muslim women explained that head coverings can serve religious purposes for some women, but may also be a practical or comfort choice for others. Canadian author and English teacher Suzanne Abdelhaq recommended soft jersey fabric, while others advised using a silk or satin underscarf and showed Abbott how to secure the fabric with pins.
Samiyah Intan Khoirunisah Zaily, who runs a small hijab business in Essen, Germany, offered to send Abbott free scarves. Other users offered to contribute toward shipping costs, and one person offered a video call to teach her how to style a hijab comfortably.
The support extended beyond headscarves. As Abbott’s story spread online, donations to her fundraiser increased, helping ease financial pressure related to her car repairs and the care of her three children. Abbott said the experience “turned my life completely around.”
Experts and commenters noted that the exchange highlighted an important distinction: a headscarf is not always a religious statement, and Abbott’s respectful request was met with solidarity rather than exclusion. The episode has been widely praised as an example of religious respect, mutual understanding and human compassion.

🇷🇺 **PUTIN ARRIVES IN CHINA FOR APEC SUMMIT AHEAD OF HISTORIC TRUMP–XI–PUTIN MEETING**

Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, November 18, to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit and prepare for a landmark trilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Putin's arrival comes ahead of the first-ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the world's three major powers, scheduled for November 19 on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

### 🤝 WHAT WILL THE THREE LEADERS DISCUSS?

According to official statements and diplomatic briefings, the discussions are expected to focus on:

- **Nuclear disarmament:** Reducing global nuclear weapons stockpiles and addressing strategic stability.
- **US–China relations:** Trade tensions, tariffs and economic cooperation.
- **Ukraine war:** The broader international security situation, although Ukraine's role in the talks remains uncertain.
- **Middle East:** Regional tensions and the wider implications of the Iran conflict.

### 🌍 WHY DOES THIS MEETING MATTER?

The gathering brings together Washington, Beijing and Moscow at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions and competition over global influence.

For Putin, the visit also offers an opportunity for direct diplomatic engagement with Western leadership despite continuing sanctions against Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.

The White House has indicated that nuclear weapons reduction will be among the subjects discussed, while officials have cautioned that an immediate agreement should not be expected.

**THE WORLD WILL BE WATCHING:** Can Trump, Putin and Xi find common ground on nuclear security and international stability, or will their competing strategic interests limit the outcome?

text:
In case you missed today's MLB hot stove news and rumors, here's everything you need to know:

🚨 BIGGEST NEWS

▸ David Bednar ACCEPTED the Yankees' qualifying offer and is back for 2027 on a one-year, $23.15M deal (via @JeffPassan). That's now the highest average salary for a reliever in MLB history, just past Edwin Díaz's $23M a year with the Dodgers. 35 saves and a 2.47 ERA this season. ( Happy to have you back :)

▸ He and Twins catcher Ryan Jeffers were the only two of the eight QO guys to take it.

⚾️ YANKEES

▸ The Yankees added RHP Carlos Lagrange, LHP Kyle Carr and OF Garrett Martin to the 40-man roster, protecting them from the Rule 5 Draft. Lagrange struck out 85 in 64.1 innings at Triple-A, Martin went 24 HR and 18 SB in 71 games between Double-A and Triple-A, and Carr posted 11.2 K/9 at Double-A. Left exposed: Facundo, Arias, Avina, Serna, Reyzelman and Antonio Gomez (via @ChrisKirschner). (No way they were risking Lagrange.)

▸ The Yankees made Jonathan Loáisiga an offer, reportedly for one year (via @RandyJMiller). He's looking for three years in the $18-20M range. 2.42 ERA in 67 innings for Arizona this year.

▸ They're also working to bring back Paul Blackburn. A rival exec has heard the Red Sox want veteran middle relief, with Blackburn and Loáisiga both potential fits (via @ChrisCotillo and @Sean_McAdam). Blackburn had a 1.59 ERA in 85 innings.

▸ The Rockies are open to moving Hunter Goodman, maybe even more than they were at the deadline, but they'd want a monster return (via @Ken_Rosenthal). The Yankees talked to Colorado about him back in July. 41 HR this year, and 25 of them came away from Coors. He was a Silver Slugger finalist at catcher tonight; Gabriel Moreno took it.

▸ The Yankees claimed RHP Chase Hampton off waivers from the Orioles. The 2022 draftee is back after getting claimed by Washington, St. Louis and Baltimore since September. He struck out 145 in 106.2 innings in 2023, then missed all of 2025 after Tommy John.

⚾️ SILVER SLUGGERS

▸ Ben Rice lost the AL DH Silver Slugger to Yordan Alvarez. Rice had 41 HR and an .897 OPS; Alvarez hit .316/.432/.601 with 42 HR and a 1.033 OPS. (Can't argue with Yordan. Still, 41 homers is a monster year from Rice.)

▸ Cody Bellinger was a finalist in the AL outfield, but those awards went to Randy Arozarena, Riley Greene and Chase DeLauter. Arozarena won his first Silver Slugger a few hours after declining Seattle's $23.15M QO. The Yankees checked in on him last week (via @JonHeyman). .865 OPS, 26 HR and 26 SB this year, and he's gone 20/20 six straight seasons.

▸ Brandon Lowe took the NL award at second base after turning down Pittsburgh's QO. 35 HR and an .824 OPS in 150 games. A lefty power bat at second still makes a lot of sense for the Yankees, but whoever signs him gives up a draft pick.

▸ Also tonight: Kyle Schwarber won NL DH after tying for the MLB home run title with 45. Jake Bauers, who just signed with Boston, took the NL utility award. Kevin McGonigle won AL utility. The Astros and Cubs won the team awards.

⚾️ METS

▸ The Mets were the first of six teams to sit down with Tarik Skubal, meeting him in Orange County. The Dodgers, Padres, Blue Jays and two mystery teams also got meetings, and he's expected to land a record deal before the Dec. 1 lockout (via @JonHeyman). 2.72 ERA and 186 K this year between Detroit and LA. (Two mystery teams. Interesting.)

⚾️ QO DECISIONS

▸ Five guys turned down the $23.15M QO: Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Brandon Lowe, Adrián Morejón and Trevor Rogers (via @Alden_Gonzalez). Whoever signs them now gives up draft pick compensation.

▸ Quick numbers on the rest: Suzuki had an .841 OPS with 26 HR, and Morejón, considered the top reliever on the market (via @Feinsand), struck out 107 in 86 innings with a 2.83 ERA. (Somebody's getting PAID.)

⚾️ WHITE SOX

▸ Dustin May got three years and $52.5M from Chicago (via @ByRobertMurray). He had a 4.70 ERA in 145.2 innings between St. Louis and Milwaukee this year. (Mid-rotation arms just got EXPENSIVE.)

⚾️ RED SOX

▸ Boston cleared a 40-man spot for Jake Bauers by trading lefty Raymond Burgos to the A's for righty Kenya Huggins (via @ChrisCotillo).

▸ Teams are still poking around on Jarren Duran. The Padres are doing background work and the Mariners and Phillies have done their due diligence too (via @ChrisCotillo and @Sean_McAdam).

▸ With a crowded 40-man and lockout uncertainty, the Red Sox added no prospects before the Rule 5 deadline, leaving Blake Wehunt exposed (via @ChrisCotillo).

⚾️ AROUND THE LEAGUE

▸ Teams locked in their Rule 5 protections tonight. The Nationals DFA'd former All-Star Josiah Gray to add top prospects Jarlin Susana and Travis Sykora. The Brewers protected former Mets first-rounder Jett Williams, and the Mets added infielder Jefferson Rojas to their 40-man.

$23.15M is a LOT for one year of a reliever. Still, there's zero long-term risk and the Yankees keep their closer. Bring Blackburn back, add one more real arm, and this pen is in good shape.

Follow us for more updates :)

🇮🇳 ENERGY-MISSION MACHINERIES (EMMIL): ORDER INFLOW RISES 16%, BUT H1 PROFITABILITY REMAINS UNDER PRESSURE

17 November 2026 | H1 FY27 Investor Presentation
1/10 | THE BIG PICTURE

Energy-Mission Machineries (India) Ltd. manufactures high-precision sheet-metal forming machinery, including CNC press brakes, shearing machines, hydraulic presses and plate-rolling machines.
H1 FY27 delivered:
• Order inflow: ₹91.55 Cr, up 15.6% YoY
• Closing order book: ₹62.27 Cr
• Standalone revenue: ₹80.26 Cr, up 6.5%
• Standalone EBITDA: ₹10.65 Cr, down 6.5%
• Standalone PAT: ₹5.54 Cr, down 16.1%

The business is growing, but earnings growth has not yet caught up.

2/10 | STANDALONE FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE
H1 FY27 vs H1 FY26:
• Revenue: ₹80.26 Cr vs ₹75.35 Cr | +6.5%
• EBITDA: ₹10.65 Cr vs ₹11.38 Cr | -6.5%
• EBITDA margin: 13.27% vs 15.11%
• PBT: ₹7.46 Cr vs ₹8.89 Cr | -16.1%
• PAT: ₹5.54 Cr vs ₹6.60 Cr | -16.1%
• EPS: ₹4.89 vs ₹5.82
Revenue growth is positive, but lower operating profitability and higher depreciation and interest costs have weighed on earnings.
3/10 | CONSOLIDATED PERFORMANCE
H1 FY27 consolidated numbers:

• Revenue: ₹80.86 Cr vs ₹75.85 Cr | +6.6%
• EBITDA: ₹9.99 Cr vs ₹11.23 Cr | -11.0%
• EBITDA margin: 12.36% vs 14.81%
• PBT: ₹6.52 Cr vs ₹8.66 Cr | -24.7%
• PAT: ₹4.49 Cr vs ₹6.42 Cr | -30.1%
• EPS: ₹3.95 vs ₹5.67

The consolidated earnings decline is sharper than the standalone decline. This deserves close monitoring as the subsidiary operations scale up.
4/10 | ORDER BOOK: THE GROWTH VISIBILITY

The order pipeline strengthened during H1 FY27.

• Opening order book: ₹47.23 Cr
• Fresh orders received: ₹91.55 Cr
• Orders executed: ₹76.50 Cr
• Closing unexecuted order book: ₹62.27 Cr
Order inflow increased approximately 15.6% YoY from ₹79.17 Cr.
The closing order book is around 0.77 times H1 revenue. Conversion of this pipeline into timely dispatches and revenue will be critical.
5/10 | BACKWARD INTEGRATION: A KEY MARGIN LEVER
The company has operationalised its wholly owned subsidiary, EM Press Form Solutions, at Sanand.
The 5,000 sq. metre facility has been operational since June 2026.
Key developments:
• In-house manufacturing of electrical enclosures, control-panel boxes, covers and fabricated components.
• New laser-cutting and powder-coating capabilities.
• Facility expected to support approximately 30–40% of backward-integration requirements.
• Lower dependence on external job workers and vendors.
Job-work expenses declined from ₹3.89 Cr in H2 FY26 to ₹2.85 Cr in H1 FY27.
Job work as a percentage of revenue declined from 4.6% to 3.5%.
Management is targeting a 16–18% reduction in absolute job-work expenses in FY27 versus FY26.

6/10 | MANUFACTURING CAPACITY EXPANSION

Installed manufacturing capacity has increased from 900 to 1,500 machines annually.
That represents a 66.7% increase in capacity.

The company operates manufacturing facilities at Anand and Sanand, with a combined manufacturing footprint of approximately 2.6 lakh sq. ft.

The strategic priority is now to ramp up utilisation, improve throughput and extract operating leverage from the expanded capacity.
Higher capacity alone does not guarantee higher returns. Utilisation and order execution will determine the economics.
7/10 | EXPORTS AND INTERNATIONAL EXPANSION
Energy Mission Machineries USA Inc. is the company's wholly owned international marketing subsidiary.
Its US presence includes:
• Headquarters in Newark, Delaware.
• Sales and service office in Orange City, California.
• Partnership with Bud's Equipment for stronger West Coast coverage.
• Distribution ambitions across the USA, Canada and Latin America.
The company participated in FABTECH 2026 in Las Vegas and reported new orders arising from the exhibition.
H1 FY27 exports contributed approximately 3% of revenue, with sales to the USA, UAE and Nepal.
International expansion offers an opportunity, but export contribution remains relatively small today.
8/10 | PRODUCT MIX AND BUSINESS POSITIONING
Approximately 73% of H1 FY27 product revenue came from hydraulic press-brake machines.

The company also manufactures:
• Hydraulic shearing machines
• Hydraulic presses
• CNC plate-rolling machines
• Machinery parts, servicing and spares

Other business strengths:
• 7,568+ machines installed
• 350+ employees
• Approximately 400 machine variants
• Around 30% of orders from repeat customers
• Products sold across 20+ Indian states
The installed base creates opportunities for repeat orders, servicing and spare-parts revenue.

9/10 | BALANCE SHEET: ITEMS TO MONITOR

Consolidated H1 FY27 balance-sheet indicators:
• Total assets: ₹166.81 Cr
• Trade receivables: ₹16.48 Cr
• Inventory: ₹80.82 Cr
• Cash and cash equivalents: ₹0.68 Cr
• Long-term borrowings: ₹11.31 Cr
• Short-term borrowings: ₹21.80 Cr
• Total equity: ₹100.60 Cr
Inventory is a significant component of current assets, while reported cash balances are relatively modest.
Investors should track inventory conversion, operating cash flow, receivable collection and borrowings alongside reported profits.

10/10 | MANAGEMENT TARGETS AND INVESTMENT VIEW

The company has outlined the following three-year targets:

• Revenue CAGR: 18–20%
• EBITDA margin: 13–15%
• PAT margin: 6–8%
The investment thesis rests on four execution drivers:

Converting the ₹62.27 Cr order book into revenue.

Improving utilisation of the expanded 1,500-machine capacity.

Delivering sustainable savings through backward integration.
Scaling exports and the international distribution network.
THE BOTTOM LINE
EMMIL has encouraging order momentum, a larger manufacturing footprint and a clear backward-integration strategy.
However, H1 FY27 earnings show margin pressure, declining PAT and a need to improve cash conversion.

The next few quarters should establish whether capacity expansion and in-house manufacturing translate into stronger margins and return ratios.

Growth visibility is improving. The quality of earnings and cash flows still needs to prove itself.

text:
Moral Authority
Loyalty, Care, and the Fitness of Ethical Life

Abstract 
This post argues that social justice is the habituated capacity of a concrete ethical order to form persons and sustain itself across generations. Drawing on Hegel’s account of *Sittlichkeit* in the *Philosophy of Right*, Aristotle’s analysis of the household, the Confucian sequence of self-cultivation and family regulation, Josiah Royce’s philosophy of loyalty, and the ethics of care, it maintains that the complementary family is the primary site of this formation. The individual is socially constituted and therefore secondary to the order that makes practical identity possible. Justice consists in the consistent observance of role-specific obligations that preserve transmission and vitality, not in the equalization of outcomes.

Introduction  
A persistent feature of modern Western political thought is the tendency to treat the individual as the primary subject of justice. This emphasis has produced the central achievements of classical liberalism: equal legal personhood, rights enforceable against arbitrary power, and the discipline of general rules. Yet when the same priority is extended to every domain, the relationships that actually constitute persons are reduced to instruments or obstacles. Households, differentiated roles, and practices of transmission appear justified only insofar as they serve or equalize pre-given individual claims.  

The argument developed here reverses that order of evaluation while retaining the liberal constraint of general law. Justice stands to a social order as virtue stands to a life: it is the habituated fitness that enables the order to form its members and reproduce the conditions of flourishing. The self is situated from the outset; its integrity is realized through loyal participation in concrete bonds, beginning with the family. Hegel’s *Philosophy of Right* provides the systematic framework, Royce specifies the structure of genuine devotion, and the ethics of care supplies the phenomenology of particular obligation. The result is a conception of social justice scaled to the communities that form us.

1. Ethical Life and the Limits of Individual Primacy  
Hegel’s *Philosophy of Right* rejects the picture of agents whose identities precede their relations. Abstract right and morality are indispensable moments, yet freedom becomes actual only in *Sittlichkeit*, “the Idea of freedom as the living Good” that has become an existing world (§142). The first moment of this order is the family, “the immediate substantiality of spirit,” whose principle is love and in which one exists as a member rather than as an independent person (§158). Marriage, family property, and the education of children complete this unity; its dissolution is the transition into civil society, not its negation.  

Aristotle’s *Politics* I.2 offers a parallel analysis. The household arises by nature from the union required for daily needs and the continuation of the species; villages and the *polis* develop from it. Although the completed political community is prior in the order of self-sufficiency, it is composed of households and presupposes their internal differentiation. The *Great Learning* states the same sequence from another tradition: those who would order the state must first regulate their families, and self-cultivation is the root for everyone from the Son of Heaven to the common people. These texts do not abolish individual agency. They locate it inside an ethical order that is already underway.

2. Loyalty and Care as the Medium of Formation  
Royce’s *Philosophy of Loyalty* defines loyalty as “the willing and practical and thoroughgoing devotion of a person to a cause.” The cause is ordinarily a community or an ideal realized in a community. Genuine loyalty is distinguished by three stipulations: it is freely sustained by the person’s will, it can harmonize with other loyalties (“loyalty to loyalty”), and it orients the agent toward a good that exceeds private satisfaction. On this account, communities possess a moral reality of their own; individuals achieve practical identity by binding themselves to them.  

The ethics of care, articulated by Noddings and Gilligan, describes how such binding is lived. Obligations arise first toward particular persons in non-substitutable relationships. Care is the habituated practice of attentiveness and responsiveness that maintains the specific goods of those relationships. It cannot be exhaustively translated into impartial rules that abstract from history and station. Inside the family, complementary roles and intergenerational duties are the primary practices through which both loyalty and care are acquired. Recognition, in this setting, is the acknowledgment of persons in the stations those practices define.

3. Justice as the Fitness of the Order  
Once the individual is understood as constituted by ethical relations, justice is the capacity of those relations to endure and to form successive generations. Role-specific standards are applied uniformly within each relationship: parents, spouses, and children are held to the obligations proper to their stations. Differences in outcome that follow from these differentiated standards are not, by themselves, evidence of injustice. Injury consists in the failure of roles, the mismatch of names and functions, or the erosion of the household’s formative power—damage to the order’s reproductive fitness.  

Institutions beyond the household are warranted to the extent that they secure the external conditions of this fitness without dissolving its internal form. Equal legal personhood remains necessary as a barrier to arbitrary power, yet it does not require that every ethical distinction be renegotiated in the direction of identical standing. Activism consistent with the account therefore concentrates on the cultivation and repair of specific bonds of loyalty and care, and it evaluates success by the stability of transmission rather than by the progressive removal of differentiated outcomes.

Objections  
The charge that an organic criterion licenses domination is met by Royce’s own stipulations: a cause that cannot harmonize with other loyalties or that rests on mere force fails the test of genuine devotion. Arbitrary authority is thereby excluded. The claim that role differentiation is incompatible with liberal rights overlooks Hegel’s explicit mediation: abstract right constrains external interference while *Sittlichkeit* supplies the positive ethical content those rights presuppose. Finally, the insistence that justice requires convergence of outcomes assumes the individualist scale under dispute. When justice is indexed to the fitness of an order of differentiated roles, unequal results under consistent standards are the expected consequence, not a rebuttal.

Conclusion  
Social justice, understood as the habituated fitness of ethical life, neither discards the individual nor subordinates every institution to pre-social claims. Hegel’s *Philosophy of Right*, read alongside Aristotle, the *Great Learning*, Royce, and the ethics of care, yields a coherent alternative in which persons are formed by loyal participation in concrete bonds and in which the complementary household stands as the immediate root of order. General laws continue to limit power; they do not replace the moral substance those laws protect. The practical task is to sustain the relationships on which formation and transmission depend.

Bibliography

Aristotle. *Nicomachean Ethics*. Translated by Terence Irwin. 2nd ed. Indianapolis: Hackett, 1999.  
Gilligan, Carol. *In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women’s Development*. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1982.

*The Great Learning*. Translated by James Legge. In *The Chinese Classics*, vol. 1. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1893.

A majority of U.S. states continue to fall short of religious freedom protections, according to a key watchdog group.

The Napa Legal Institute’s 2026 Faith and Freedom Index, released on Nov. 16, shows more than half of states scoring below 50% on key measures related to freedom of religion.

The index reviews several factors including state constitutional religious protections, religious freedom for faith-based employers, and whether or not a state constitution includes a “Blaine amendment,” a feature of many state-level constitutions that prohibits public funding of religious education.

Just two states on this year’s index scored above 80% on the list’s metrics: Kansas at 87% and Alabama at 94%. Michigan scored the lowest for the second year in a row, at 24%.

In a press release announcing the list, the institute noted that religious freedom scores “do not neatly fall along partisan lines.”

“There are ‘blue states’ that have some important religious freedom and regulatory protections for faith-based nonprofits, as well as ‘red states’ that have much room for improvement,” the organization said.

It noted that heavily Democratic New York received a higher score than traditionally Republican North Dakota. States like Hawaii and Maine, meanwhile, have “stronger employment law protections” for religious employers than do states like South Dakota and West Virginia.

Napa senior counsel Frank DeVito said it is “crucial” for states to create legal frameworks that allow religious organizations “to focus on their mission rather than time and resource-consuming legal compliance requirements.”

“Every good state law that helps rather than hinders the work of religious organizations is a victory,” he said. He urged voters to “consider how the laws in their states burden religion when they cast their votes.”

In its ranking of Michigan as the worst for religious liberty, the institute said the state has “several laws that are burdensome to faith-based nonprofits operating in the state,” including a Blaine amendment. It also has no state-level Religious Freedom Restoration Act and offers no protections for religious exercise during a state of emergency.

The group described Alabama, meanwhile, as “one of the best places to operate a faith-based nonprofit in the United States,” though as with Michigan the state constitution incorporates a Blaine amendment against religious education.

The Napa list also includes a “regulatory freedom” rundown, where most states score much higher than their respective results on the religious freedom index.
