text:
What would happen when a crowd start shorting a company after they release their IPO?

When a crowd piles into shorting a newly public company, a few things tend to happen, and they interact in interesting ways.

Immediate price pressure. Heavy short selling pushes the price down, since shorts are selling borrowed shares. But right after an IPO this is harder than it sounds, because of the next point.

Shorting is constrained early on.

Borrow availability is scarce. Only a small float trades at first, and most shares are held by the underwriters’ clients, so few shares are available to borrow.
Borrow costs are high. Fees can run into double or even triple digits annualized, which makes holding a short expensive.
Quiet period and lock-ups. Insiders and early investors are typically locked up for around 90 to 180 days, which keeps the float small. That limits supply for borrowing, though it also means a wave of share supply when the lock-up expires, which shorts often try to time.
Stabilization. Underwriters usually hold a greenshoe (overallotment) option. If the price dips below the offer price, they can buy shares in the market to support it, which blunts early short pressure.

The squeeze risk. Because the float is small and borrow is tight, a heavily shorted new stock is vulnerable to a short squeeze. If the price rises instead of falls, shorts must buy back shares to cover losses or meet margin calls, and that buying pushes the price up further, forcing more covering. This can produce spikes far above any fundamental value. Retail-driven squeezes like GameStop in 2021 are the famous example, and some recent IPOs have seen similar dynamics.

Possible outcomes.

The shorts are right. The IPO was overpriced, the price falls toward fair value, and shorts profit, especially around lock-up expirations or weak earnings.
The shorts get squeezed. A small float plus a coordinated buying response sends the price up and shorts take large losses.
Volatility and noise. Prices whip around while borrow costs eat into short positions, and the price discovery is messy for weeks.

Other factors.

Short sellers’ losses are theoretically unlimited, while their gains are capped at 100%.
Regulators watch for manipulation. Coordinated shorting combined with spreading false information (“short and distort”) can be illegal, as can coordinated schemes to move a price artificially.
Naked shorting (selling without locating shares to borrow) is restricted under Regulation SHO in the US.

In practice, shorting right after an IPO is one of the riskier trades, because expensive borrow and squeeze risk often outweigh the edge, even when the valuation looks stretched. Many short sellers wait until after the lock-up expires or until the first earnings reports.

Are you asking from a market-mechanics curiosity angle, or about a specific situation?

What if the opposite happens, lets say the crows short squeeze the IPO, then switch to long squeeze when the holders start selling. Would that make the price drop?

Yes, in most cases the price would drop, and often sharply. What you're describing is a classic boom-and-bust pattern, and the second phase is where the real damage tends to happen.

Why the first phase matters. In a short squeeze, the price rises because shorts are forced to buy, not because anyone has re-valued the company. That demand is mechanical and temporary. Once the shorts have covered, the buying pressure disappears, and the price has nothing underneath it except whatever new buyers are willing to pay.

What happens when holders start selling. Several groups may sell at once:
Early buyers taking profits. Anyone who bought before or during the squeeze is sitting on large gains and has an incentive to lock them in.
Insiders and early investors. If a lock-up expires during or after the spike, a large block of new shares can hit a market that was already stretched. This is often the biggest single trigger.
Late buyers who panic. People who bought near the top start selling as the price slips, which accelerates the fall.
New short sellers. With the price far above fundamentals, shorts re-enter, adding to the downward pressure.

Why it can cascade. There's a mirror image of a squeeze here, sometimes called a long liquidation or "long squeeze." Leveraged buyers who used margin or options get margin calls as the price falls, which forces them to sell, which pushes the price down further, which triggers more margin calls. Stop-loss orders add to this. Since the float is small, there are few buyers to absorb the selling, so price moves can be violent, and gaps down are common.

How far could it fall? There's no fixed rule, but a few things shape it:
If the price was pushed far above fundamental value, it will tend to fall back toward it, and often overshoots on the way down.
If the company is genuinely strong, the price may settle at a level well above the IPO price, with the squeeze leaving a lasting re-rating. This is the exception, not the norm.
Many squeezed stocks end up below the pre-squeeze level, because the hype fades and attention moves on. GameStop is a partial exception since it settled well above its pre-squeeze level, though far below its peak. Several other 2021 meme stocks fell most or all of the way back.

One caveat. The sequence isn't guaranteed. Sometimes holders keep holding, sometimes new buyers step in, and sometimes a second squeeze happens before the collapse. But the structure you describe, mechanical buying followed by supply hitting a thin market, makes a significant drop the most likely outcome.

If you're thinking about this as a trade rather than a thought experiment, it's worth knowing that timing the top of a squeeze is extremely hard, and both sides of it have wiped out a lot of people.

text:
**James Chapter 2 (King James Version)**

1 My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.

2 For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;

3 And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool:

4 Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?

5 Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?

6 But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?

7 Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called?

8 If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well:

9 But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.

10 For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.

11 For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law.

12 So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.

13 For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.

14 What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him?

15 If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food,

16 And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?

17 Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.

18 Yea, a man may say, Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.

19 Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.

20 But wilt thou know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead?

21 Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?

22 Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?

23 And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God.

24 Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.

25 Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?

26 For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.

 King James Version (1611).

text:
The nation's winter wheat crop is showing improvement heading into dormancy, although conditions vary considerably across the Great Plains.

USDA's November 16 Crop Progress report rated 53% of winter wheat acreage in good or excellent condition as of November 15.

That represents a four-percentage-point improvement from the previous week and is eight points above the comparable rating a year earlier.

Kansas, the country's largest winter wheat-producing state, recorded one of the more encouraging changes.

Its good-to-excellent rating climbed six points to 57%.

Recent rainfall across portions of the Plains likely contributed to improved conditions, although individual fields vary with planting dates, soil moisture and local weather.

Across the state line, Oklahoma presents a different picture.

Only 35% of its winter wheat was rated good or excellent, down one point from the previous week.

That difference is important because winter wheat must establish adequate roots and plant growth before colder temperatures slow development.

Good fall establishment can help a crop withstand winter conditions and resume growth in spring.

However, a favorable November rating does not guarantee a strong harvest.

Winterkill, spring drought, late freezes, disease and grain-filling temperatures can all change the final outcome.

USDA also reported that 82% of the national winter wheat crop had emerged, slightly ahead of the five-year average of 81%.

Planting was complete in Colorado, Idaho, Nebraska and Washington, according to the latest state-level figures.

For growers, the immediate concern is getting adequate moisture into the soil before winter dormancy.

For grain buyers, the improving national ratings offer an early indication of crop potential, but production estimates remain months away.

The contrast between Kansas and Oklahoma is a reminder that statewide and national averages can conceal very different conditions on neighboring farms.

text:
You keep saying I’m “missing the point.” I understand your point. You think it looks bad. I’m asking what evidence makes it bad beyond your own assumptions.

You’re in the Washington, DC area, around the Pentagon, Walter Reed, military installations, and government offices. Why are you surprised to see disabled veterans there?

That’s like me living in Colorado Springs, surrounded by military installations, and acting shocked that military personnel and veterans are everywhere. 

For perspective, VA reported approximately 6.34 million veterans receiving disability compensation as of September 30, 2025. The country has approximately 343 million people. That’s roughly 1.8% of the population. Those are compensation recipients, not a count of DV plates or people eligible for handicap parking. 

Even if every one of those 6.34 million veterans had a vehicle with DV plates, you’d still be talking about a small share of Americans. Seeing several concentrated around military and government facilities (in DC ) shouldn’t be some kind a  mystery.

And a luxury car or lifted truck tells you absolutely nothing about the driver’s medical history. Disabled veterans don’t have to look poor or helpless to satisfy you.

You’ve offered no evidence those people improperly obtained their plates or placards. You’ve offered a parking lot observation and your personal opinion of their vehicles.

You’re blaming veterans for the “optics” of assumptions you brought to the parking lot.

What am I missing exactly?

text:
The players you need to TRADE AWAY before the fantasy football trade deadline

Trading away Bijan Robinson requires a nuanced perspective. Of course, Bijan Robinson is one of the top assets to have in fantasy, but he has his bye this week, followed by tough matchups with Minnesota and Detroit. If you need wins right now, it's logical to move Robinson for a package including an RB with a better upcoming schedule and another piece i.e. Bucky Irving etc.

Josh Jacobs is someone to consider trading away if you're a team that needs players in your lineup right now. He was inefficient before the injury, and the blocking in the run game continues to struggle. In other words, if you can't afford to roster injured players/players with byes, move off of Jacobs in exchange for someone comparable.

Breece Hall's Week 10 performance was bailed out by four receptions for 67 yards. He's on a team that'll be in tough game scripts, and his matchup in the fantasy championship is Minnesota. It's worth seeing what sort of offers you can get for him.

At this moment in time, Tyler Warren is someone to sell based solely on his remaining name value. He's on an atrocious offense, and he's the primary target for other teams to defend. See if you can get ANYTHING for him.

text:
#PublicAttention #Disinformation #Power
LEARNING TO ACCEPT
“By stratagems you shall wage war.”
— Proverbs 24:6, an old motto of the Mossad
On November 16, someone managed to make websites that millions of people visit and trust serve malicious code capable of stealing payment-card details and redirecting cryptocurrency transfers. Among those sites were the BBC, CNN, and Zoom. A visitor could type the right address, recognize the page, and still be exposed to the deception. Whoever planted the code drew on a trust that others had built.
Around the same time, a Microsoft outage left users without access to email, the United States temporarily suspended departures nationwide, and Pope Leo XIV concluded in Peru a tour announced in August. Each episode deserves to be examined on its own terms. Yet the first explanation we hear often decides where our inquiry ends. A system failed. A trip went ahead as planned. The matter has been dealt with. Once we accept those accounts, how often do we go back and ask who had the means to shape what happened, or who had a hand in deciding what we would be told about it?
My hypothesis goes beyond the idea that people in power know how to take advantage of a crisis. I think some events can be deliberately brought about, amplified, or prolonged to keep people in a state of uncertainty. That is a possibility worth investigating even when an event initially looks accidental, or appears to have unfolded outside anyone’s political control. The overlap of these episodes leaves open who caused each one and whether anyone coordinated them. I am asking whether the production of disruption itself can be a method of governing.
Such a method could serve two purposes. The first is immediate. While people are absorbed in getting home, recovering their email, or following the images of a papal visit, decisions that would otherwise draw scrutiny can pass with little attention. The second is more lasting. Repeated disruptions can teach us how to behave the next time. You cannot travel, so you wait. You cannot open your email, so you wait. When an explanation arrives, you have a practical reason to accept it and move on. You want your life back. I wonder what happens when that reasonable response to a particular emergency becomes a habit of submission. How much will we accept the next time, simply because we have learned that waiting and complying are the quickest ways to get on with our lives?
The pandemic offers a documented example of how far this can go. Reuters found that the Pentagon used fake accounts posing as Filipinos to undermine confidence in China’s Sinovac vaccine and other medical supplies. While people were trying to decide how to protect themselves, a foreign power was covertly intervening in that decision. It even manufactured some of the voices through which people were supposed to make sense of the crisis. That case gives substance to a broader question about the pandemic. What did people learn to accept under emergency conditions, who worked to shape what they believed, and which of those habits survived the emergency itself?
Ecuador offers one place to ask that question. On November 15, in the middle of an election campaign, an extension of the state of emergency took effect. It kept the constitutional protection for the privacy of correspondence suspended in the areas covered by the decree. The signed decree is public. How the power is exercised is harder to see. Who authorizes an interception? Who checks that it serves the purposes stated in the decree? What will a person whose communications were intercepted be able to find out afterward?
…/

Mr. Alaabohaye, for a man who advertises himself as a political analyst, researcher, UCL graduate, and chartered accountant, your response contains a remarkable shortage of analysis.

I raised questions concerning allegations of foreign interference in Somalia. You replied by calling me a “brainwashed Saudi subject” and advising me to prepare for the trenches.

How illuminating.

On November 17, Somalia’s own president publicly accused the UAE of undermining his country’s sovereignty, supporting armed formations outside the national command structure, and interfering in its political affairs.

These are allegations that require evidence, scrutiny, and a serious response. They are not established truths merely because a president uttered them, but neither do they disappear because an admirer of Abu Dhabi finds them inconvenient.

And what did you offer in response? Not a document. Not a counterargument. Not even a coherent explanation. Just an insult to my nationality.

As for your advice about defending the Two Holy Mosques, allow me to explain something.

Their protection is an honour that Saudi Arabia has carried with immense pride and responsibility. You mistake devotion for vulnerability when you invoke the Haramain as an insult.

I am Saudi, and I need neither your permission to defend my country’s interests nor your approval to speak against the suffering of fellow Muslims.

My concern for Somalia does not require allegiance to its president. My concern for Sudan does not require allegiance to its army. And my refusal to excuse atrocities does not require your approval.

You may disagree with every word I say. That is your right.

But the moment you abandon the argument to attack the nationality of the person making it, you reveal far more about the limits of your reasoning than about his.

Your biography is full of qualifications. Your reply, unfortunately, arrived without a single argument.

And there is a final irony worth appreciating: you call me brainwashed while apparently expecting a Saudi to remain silent whenever the policies of a foreign government are questioned.

I answer to my conscience, my principles, and my country.

Whose approval are you so anxious to preserve?

text:
Kulgam Encounter | 18 Nov 2026
Joint forces of J&K Police, Army and CRPF have established contact with and cornered LeT commander Mohammed Lateef Bhat in the Zangalpora area of Kulgam district early Wednesday (~4 AM). Exchange of fire is underway. Security forces are appealing for surrender; Bhat has refused.

Re-cap of events:

10 Nov: Lateef Bhat (22, Khrewan village, Kulgam; A-category, ~₹15 lakh bounty; repeatedly described as the only surviving local terrorist in the Valley) and associate Umar Nisar Dar conducted reconnaissance at Mir Bazar, Akhran, Hablish and Kilam. CCTV later confirmed their movements.⁠

11 Nov: The pair attacked a CRPF naka at Akhran (near Mir Bazar). They approached through a tree-covered stretch and opened fire from ~50 m, injuring three CRPF personnel, then fled. Dar had reportedly provided shelter and logistical support to Bhat for 5–6 months and formally joined TRF (LeT offshoot) around the attack.⁠

16–17 Nov (Laroo/Larnoo bypass): On specific intelligence, forces intercepted the pair. Umar Nisar Dar was killed; his body was recovered. Bhat escaped the cordon, believed injured (bullet wounds), and fled into nearby orchards/forests. Intensive search (drones, dogs, cordons, door-to-door) continued for days.

18 Nov (Zangalpora): Fresh intelligence led to a search that re-established contact. Kashmir Zone Police confirmed: “Encounter started with terrorists and Joint party of JKP and SF in Kulgam.” Bhat is assessed as trapped. Forces have offered surrender; audio/video shows him rejecting it with religious statements (“Allah is enough for me,” “I have to go to Allah… Allah Hu Akbar”).⁠

Operation ongoing to capture or neutralise Bhat. No official confirmation of outcome beyond contact and ongoing exchange of fire as of early reports.

text:
I read an article by Swapan Dasgupta in *India Today*. Reading it completely changed my perspective on the media.

He wrote that a significant segment of the media is on the payroll of Pakistani intelligence—the ISI. They present news in a way that ultimately harms the nation.

He cited the 1999 hijacking of flight IC-814 as an example: the media first pressured the government by highlighting the plight of the hostages' families, and then, once the government conceded to the demands, they criticized it for doing so—all while portraying the country as weak. In both instances, they acted against the national interest.

He noted that he, too, had been offered money to write such pieces—sums so substantial that most people would find it difficult to refuse.

After that, I kept my eyes open and witnessed many such instances. For example, following the 2001 Parliament attack, our armed forces were deployed at the border, and Pakistan was under immense pressure.

The cost of maintaining its own forces on high alert was crippling Pakistan. Then, suddenly, in June 2002, several magazines simultaneously published articles claiming that the presence of our troops at the border was causing them great hardship—and that the morale of the army was declining.

Even if morale were low, such information is never shared with the enemy; it is not even acknowledged internally—instead, efforts are made to boost morale. Our soldiers are always stationed at the borders, enduring constant hardship—yet you never see articles praising them. Why, then, was their suffering suddenly brought to light?

It is clear who stood to gain from such reporting. The intent was to pressure the government into withdrawing our forces, thereby giving Pakistan a sigh of relief.

Back then, social media did not exist. Witnessing this left me feeling deeply restless and frustrated.  After leaving the armed forces, I kept searching for a platform from which I could expose this particular nature of the media.

Political parties proved to be a deeply stifling, intellectually shallow, and narrow-minded space. Not only is it difficult to find an opportunity to express one’s views there, but the credibility of these parties themselves is often questionable.

Then, following the 2008 Mumbai attacks, I took note of how the media was diverting public attention. The public’s outrage had been hijacked by the "candlelight brigade," who steered the focus toward "all politicians" and "all political parties"—a tactic designed to shield the Congress party from accountability and minimize its political fallout.

That was when my wife and I decided to create a grassroots social platform. With behind-the-scenes support from a few friends—who helped arrange a microphone and a stage—I stood at a street corner one day, accompanied by my wife and children, and began speaking out against the terror attacks, as well as the collusion between the government and the media.

A crowd began to gather. The event had no pre-set agenda; it was entirely spontaneous. The first gathering was a great success, and we continued to hold similar events at various street corners every Sunday. Thanks to the efforts of some friends, this platform—now known as "Rashtrachetna" (National Consciousness)—remains active in Jamshedpur to this day.

Then came social media. Platforms like Facebook and Twitter have completely laid bare the true nature of the media. What once required spending an entire day and five hundred to a thousand rupees just to reach two or three hundred people, can now be amplified through one’s network of five thousand friends to reach hundreds of thousands.

Today, the role of shaping public opinion has shifted away from a compromised mainstream media and into the hands of the people themselves.

text:
A friend of mine posted this Jeopardy question on SM. 

“On Jeopardy the other night, the Final Jeopardy clue asked how many steps the guard takes during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. All three contestants missed it.

The answer is 21.”

I didn’t know a lot of details about this topic, so I turned to my handy educator, Grok.   I was so humbled and touched at what I have learned, I decided to share it here. 

Sentinels of the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment (The Old Guard) take exactly 21 steps down the 63-foot black mat, then pause 21 seconds facing east and 21 seconds facing north before repeating the sequence. The number 21 represents the 21-gun salute—the highest honor the nation can bestow. Their gloves are lightly moistened so they never lose their grip on the rifle. The rifle is always carried on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb, so the sentinel stands between the Unknowns and any possible threat.

A sentinel has been on duty every minute of every day since July 1937. The watch has never been broken—not for weather, war, or government shutdowns. During Hurricane Isabel in 2003, the guards were offered permission to seek shelter for the first time in the Tomb’s history. They stayed at their posts.
They volunteer for one of the most selective and demanding duties in the U.S. Army. Most who begin training do not complete it. Those who do must master flawless ceremonial movements, memorize extensive history of the Tomb and Arlington National Cemetery, and know the locations of hundreds of notable graves. After months of perfection they earn the Tomb Guard Identification Badge—one of the rarest awards in the Army (more than 600 have been issued since the late 1950s). It can be revoked at any time, even years later, for conduct that discredits the Tomb.

They walk in extreme heat, cold, rain, and snow. Their shoes have thick soles and metal heel plates that produce a sharp, precise click when they halt. Their uniforms are inspected to perfection. Men must be between 5’10” and 6’4”; women between 5’8” and 6’2”, with a proportionate build. Women have earned the badge as well.

Among those buried at Arlington whose stories the sentinels learn are President William Howard Taft, Audie Murphy (the most decorated soldier of World War II), and boxer Joe Louis.

They live by the Sentinel’s Creed:

“My dedication to this sacred duty is total and whole-hearted. In the responsibility bestowed on me never will I falter. And with dignity and perseverance my standard will remain perfection. Through the years of diligence and praise and the discomforts of the elements, I will walk my tour in humble reverence to the best of my ability. It is he who commands the respect I protect, his bravery that made us so proud. Surrounded by well meaning crowds by day, alone in the thoughtful peace of night, this soldier will in honored glory rest under my eternal vigilance.”

Since 1937 the watch has never been broken. The sentinels measure their success by a single standard: perfection in the presence of the Unknowns.

Eternal rest grant them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.

I don’t often ask people to reshare posts, but I would be honored if this one reached as many people as possible. We should always feel proud of the men and women who serve.

text:
Lately, I’ve had quite a few conversations with people who ask me the same question: “With so many alternative education programs opening across South Florida, aren’t you worried about the competition?”

It’s a fair question. Especially when you consider the challenges we’re facing with declining student enrollment, economic uncertainty, and an increasingly competitive educational landscape.

But my answer is always the same: Absolutely not.

I embrace competition. In fact, I welcome it.

Competition challenges me to think bigger, innovate, improve, and continuously raise the standards of what we offer families. It pushes me to become a better educator, entrepreneur, and leader.

I believe that as leaders in education, we have a responsibility to push boundaries, challenge traditional models, and earn the trust of parents through our actions, results, and commitment to their children.

Families deserve choices. They deserve transparency, accountability, and educational environments that genuinely meet their children’s needs.

The goal should never be to eliminate competition. It should be to become better because of it.

And if the growth of alternative education in South Florida means more families have access to meaningful educational opportunities, then I consider that a win for all of us.

There is room for innovation, but there should never be room for complacency when it comes to educating children.

text:
“To balance their budgets in this new landscape, many districts will need to right-size, trimming payrolls and facilities. However, because layoffs and school closures are so painful, school district administrators often delay decisions as long as possible.

To safeguard taxpayer dollars, state policymakers should adopt policies that steward public funds and increase transparency. Most states aren’t transparent about how many school buildings are underused. States should publish data identifying unused, underutilized or vacant school buildings in every school district.

Moreover, states should eliminate declining enrollment provisions that base education funding on outdated student counts. These policies cost taxpayers more because they fund “ghost students” who have exited the public school system by graduating or enrolling in non-traditional public schools. Education funding should be based on current or prior-year enrollments, ensuring district budgets reflect actual student counts.

Additionally, policymakers can ensure that facilities slated for closure continue to benefit local student populations. Charter schools should be able to purchase, lease, or co-locate in underutilized district school buildings, as they do in Indiana and Florida. Those states offer strong models for maximizing publicly funded infrastructure in ways that benefit school children, regardless of where they go to school.

School closures are difficult for students and communities, but public school enrollment declines and districts’ financial situations are unlikely to improve, so these challenges must be addressed.”

text:
Runway-free aerial logistics just hit U.S. soil with 550 lbs of pure electric lifting muscle.

AIR VEV has officially deployed its AIR 120D autonomous cargo eVTOL to its Florida headquarters for flight demonstrations. Built on an all-electric, 8-motor coaxial quadcopter architecture paired with fixed wings, it skips heavy tilt-rotor mechanisms to keep weight low and reliability high. During forward cruise, its 36-foot folding wings generate roughly 60% of the lift, stretching battery efficiency while cutting emissions and noise compared to fuel-burning helicopters. Guided by triple-redundant LTE, SATCOM, and tactical radio links, it hauls 550 lbs inside a 70-cubic-foot modular bay without a pilot or runway.

Use cases span rapid humanitarian disaster relief, offshore ship-to-shore resupply, rural mid-mile freight, and contested defense logistics.

For aviation and autonomy engineers: does avoiding mechanical tilt-rotors in favor of fixed-wing aerodynamic lift sharing offer the best reliability-to-range trade-off for Group 4 cargo UAS?
Watch a quick visual overview of the milestone in The pilotless electric cargo aircraft that hauls 550 pounds without a runway to see how the AIR 120D platform fits into runway-independent logistics.

text:
CHA @ LAL: Lean Charlotte +7.5: new Lakers absences and sharp money, but the line already moved

Verdict: Lean Charlotte +7.5 for a half unit. 

Walker Kessler's new absence weakens the Lakers where Charlotte is strongest, and the market has moved hard toward the Hornets, but that three-point move has already taken most of the value.

Picks
• CHA +7.5 -110 (Hard Rock Bet) · 0.5u

Two Lakers starters who are not in the recent numbers are out tonight. Walker Kessler (C) played Nov 15 and had started all 14 games, so his 10.9 rebounds a game (27% of the Lakers' boards) are missing from every recent split. Austin Reaves (G) scores 24.7 points (20% of team points) and has missed only the Phoenix game. The Lakers are 2-0 without Reaves, but they have never played a game without Kessler this season. Charlotte has been without Kon Knueppel (G) and Dennis Schroder (G) since Nov 8, so those losses are already in its recent form. Its -10.8 season margin barely changed with or without Schroder.

Kessler's absence hits the unit where Charlotte is elite. The Hornets rebound 33.1% of their own misses, second in the league, and the Lakers already ranked 28th in defensive rebounding (68.4%) with him. Charlotte also takes 44.8 threes a game (#1) against a defense that allows 40.9 attempts (27th) at 36.6% (23rd). That is a high-variance shot profile, which helps an underdog. On the road the Hornets lose by an average of 6.7 points (n=6), against 14.3 at home. The real weakness is ball security. Charlotte commits 19.4 turnovers a game (#30), and the Lakers lead the league in steals at 11.0. The Hornets gave it away 27 times at Phoenix on Nov 12 and still covered +6.5.

The market agrees with the injury read. The spread opened LAL -10.5 and sits at -7.5 even though the Lakers have 85% of tickets and 77% of the money. The moneyline went from -451 to -296. Pinnacle has backed Charlotte all pre-game, moving from +9 to +7. Your systems line up on the same side: seven of them back Charlotte at +6.5, with a median 55% hit rate and +4.7% ROI, and the top two hit 63% and 61%. Only six fire on the Lakers.

The price is the catch. At Pinnacle's +7 -101, CHA +7.5 (-110 Hard Rock Bet) grades out slightly negative (-3.0% EV at the best price). The three-point move has already absorbed most of the injury edge.

The quarter markets do not offer a cleaner angle. The Lakers score 31.7 first-quarter points (#1) against Charlotte's 24.8 (#29), which rules out early Hornets plays. Charlotte's 21.1 fourth-quarter points (#30) argue against CHA +2.5 (-106 FanDuel) in the second half. The full game is the only market where your systems, the reverse move and the rebounding mismatch all point the same way.

The best case for the Lakers: they have the league's top offense (121.2 per 100), Luka Doncic (G) just scored 43, they have won 8 straight and they are 10-4 ATS. Charlotte's offense (100.3) is the league's worst.

That keeps this to a half-unit lean on CHA +7.5 (-110 Hard Rock Bet) at Hard Rock's -110, well below the -119 consensus. If you want a safer leg for a combo, CHA +8.5 (-130 ESPN BET) buys the extra point.

text:
Do Fletch NOLA Blues/Tony Adamo
They unearthed him from the Delta dust/ Do Fletch, a name whispered on the wind, in a rusted tone/  Born and bred in NOLA's humid heart, A city sculpted by sorrow, torn apart, then rebuilt from the start/  Do Fletch not a singer, not an artist, not a star in the sky, but a conduit, a vessel, for the blues to cry/  His voice, a Mississippi moan, rising slow and thick, like the river itself, carrying history/ He didn't sing the blues, he bled them onto the stage/   Each note is a memory, etched deep in a man's age. Pain poured from his pores, a vintage Bourbon stain/  Every tremor in his throat, a forgotten hurricane/ He sang of levees broken, promises betrayed/  of rent past due, and his future slowly fading away/  He sang of love lost in the back alleys and grime, of the weight of generations pressing down on his time/   His voice, a deep-telling blues, the kind that crawls under your skin, A symphony of sorrow, a chorus of what might have been/  He didn't offer hope, he didn't offer light, He offered truth, raw and unflinching, in the dead of the night/  So listen close, to the ghost in his gravelly tone/  Do Fletch, rediscovered, no longer alone/  Let his pain be a reminder, a lesson learned in hard sorrow, that the blues ain't dead, just waiting to rise again/ Nuff said/

text:
Republicans cannot pass their own agenda or force major outcomes on their own. With the numbers you referenced (roughly 21 Republicans in the 60-seat House, matching the post-2026 election projections of about 39 Democrats–21 Republicans), they are a clear minority. Democrats also hold the Senate (projected ~19–11) and the governorship (Tina Kotek), creating a full Democratic trifecta. 
Current power balance
•  House: Democrats control a strong majority (and three-fifths supermajority territory). Simple majority is 31 seats; three-fifths for tax increases is 36.
•  Senate: Democrats hold a similar advantage.
•  Democrats already had three-fifths majorities going into the 2026 election and expanded them. That lets them pass tax measures and many other bills along party lines without any Republican votes. 
What Republicans can do
They are limited to opposition and leverage tactics rather than affirmative power:
•  Debate, amendments, and publicity — They can force discussion, offer alternative proposals, highlight problems, and try to peel off moderate Democrats on specific issues. This is mostly about shaping the narrative and the record.
•  Walkouts / quorum denial — Oregon Republicans have used this tool in the past to stall bills by denying a quorum. Larger Democratic majorities make it harder (more Democrats would need to be absent or the math changes), but it remains a possible pressure tactic on high-stakes items.
•  Committee work and negotiation — Ranking minority members can influence details, slow things down, or extract concessions when Democrats want broader support or to avoid looking purely partisan.
•  Outside the Capitol — Public pressure, media, local organizing, county-level work (relevant in more Republican areas like Douglas County), and preparing for the next election cycle.
Bottom line
Republicans cannot “make anything happen” in the sense of advancing their preferred legislation or blocking Democratic priorities that have unified majority support. Their role is primarily to oppose, delay, amend at the margins, and make the majority accountable. When Democrats are united, the minority’s practical power is limited. When Democrats split or face public backlash, Republican pressure and publicity can matter more. That is the standard dynamic of a durable minority in a one-party-dominant legislature

text:
Most Americans think FLORIDA and CALIFORNIA offer the same beach experience.

Sunshine. Sand. Palm trees. Ocean.

But there’s one difference that surprises visitors every summer.

In Florida, you can walk into the ocean and enjoy warm water for hours.

In California, you can have an 80°F summer day, step into the Pacific, and immediately regret your decision.

Why?

California’s coastline is influenced by the cold California Current and coastal upwelling.

Florida’s waters are generally much warmer.

But here’s where things get interesting.

FLORIDA is famous for tropical beaches, warm-water swimming, and laid-back vacations.

CALIFORNIA is famous for surfing, dramatic coastlines, and iconic beach towns.

And there’s another difference.

In Miami, you can watch the sunrise over the Atlantic.

In Malibu, you can watch the sunset over the Pacific.

TWO STATES. TWO COASTS. TWO DIFFERENT BEACH EXPERIENCES.

Now the real question:

Where would you rather spend your summer?

🔵 FLORIDA 🌴
🟠 CALIFORNIA 🌊
